units.title: Stocks and Ownership
units.tip: A stock is a share of ownership in a company. When you buy stock, you own a tiny piece of that business and can benefit if it grows in value. Stocks are bought and sold on exchanges where thousands of investors trade daily.

exercises.question: What does owning a stock mean?
exercises.answer: You own a small percentage of a company
exercises.explain: A stock is a unit of ownership. If a company has 1,000,000 shares and you own 1,000 shares, you own 0.1% of that company.
choices: You loaned money to the company
You are guaranteed a fixed return
You own a small percentage of a company

exercises.question: What is a 'share'?
exercises.answer: One unit of ownership in a company
exercises.explain: A share is the basic unit you buy and sell. Companies divide ownership into many shares to allow investors to own any sized piece.
choices: A fixed payment from the company
One unit of ownership in a company

exercises.question: If a company is worth 100 million dollars and has 10 million shares, what is one share worth?
exercises.answer: 10 dollars
exercises.explain: Dividing total company value by share count gives the price per share. 100,000,000 / 10,000,000 = 10 dollars per share.

exercises.question: What happens to your share of ownership when a company issues more shares?
exercises.answer: Your percentage ownership decreases
exercises.explain: If a company issues more shares, the total number increases. Your fixed number of shares now represents a smaller percentage of the whole.
choices: Your percentage ownership stays the same

exercises.question: What is the main reason people buy stocks?
exercises.answer: Hope that the company grows and the stock value increases
exercises.explain: Investors buy stocks expecting the company to grow, increase profits, and become more valuable. This increases the stock price and investor wealth.
choices: Hope that the company grows and the stock value increases
Companies require investors to buy shares

exercises.question: What is a stock exchange?
exercises.answer: A marketplace where stocks are bought and sold between investors
exercises.explain: Stock exchanges allow buyers and sellers to meet and trade. The price changes as supply and demand shift.
choices: A marketplace where stocks are bought and sold between investors

exercises.question: Why does a stock price change?
exercises.answer: Supply and demand: more buyers than sellers drives price up
exercises.explain: Stock prices move second-to-second based on how many people want to buy versus sell. More demand pushes price up; more selling pressure pushes it down.
choices: It stays fixed once the stock launches
The company decides to change it
Supply and demand: more buyers than sellers drives price up

exercises.question: If you buy a stock at 50 dollars and it rises to 60 dollars, how much profit do you have per share?
exercises.answer: 10 dollars
exercises.explain: Profit is the selling price minus the buying price. 60 - 50 = 10 dollars of profit per share.

exercises.question: What does it mean for a stock to be 'volatile'?
exercises.answer: Its price swings up and down frequently and by large amounts
exercises.explain: Volatile stocks have big price swings. A stable stock moves little from day to day, while a volatile stock can move a lot in a short time.
choices: Its price swings up and down frequently and by large amounts

exercises.question: If you buy 100 shares at 30 dollars per share, how much money do you spend?
exercises.answer: 3,000 dollars
exercises.explain: 100 shares times 30 dollars per share equals 3,000 dollars. Multiply share count by price per share to get total cost.

units.title: Bonds and Lending
units.tip: A bond is a loan you make to a company or government. They borrow your money, promise to pay interest, and return your original amount at maturity. Bonds tend to be less volatile than stocks, but they also tend to offer lower potential returns.

exercises.question: What is a bond?
exercises.answer: A loan where you lend money and receive interest payments
exercises.explain: A bond is an IOU. You lend money, the borrower pays you interest regularly, and returns your principal when the bond matures.
choices: An ownership stake in a company
A loan where you lend money and receive interest payments

exercises.question: Who can issue bonds?
exercises.answer: Companies and governments seeking to borrow money
exercises.explain: Bonds are issued by entities that need to raise money. A company might issue a bond to fund expansion; a government might issue a bond to finance infrastructure.
choices: Companies and governments seeking to borrow money

exercises.question: What is the 'face value' or 'principal' of a bond?
exercises.answer: The amount of money you lent, returned at maturity
exercises.explain: If you buy a 1,000 dollar bond, the face value is 1,000. That is what the borrower returns when the bond matures (reaches its end date).
choices: The amount of money you lent, returned at maturity
The price you pay to buy the bond

exercises.question: What is 'maturity' for a bond?
exercises.answer: The date when the borrower returns your principal
exercises.explain: A bond has a maturity date set when it is issued. At that date, the borrower repays your full original amount. Until then, you receive interest payments.
choices: How long you own the bond
The date the bond is issued
The date when the borrower returns your principal

exercises.question: If you own a 1,000 dollar bond with a 3% annual interest rate, how much interest do you receive each year?
exercises.answer: 30 dollars
exercises.explain: Interest is face value times rate. 1,000 * 0.03 = 30 dollars per year. This is paid to you while you own the bond.

exercises.question: What is the difference between a stock and a bond?
exercises.answer: A stock is ownership; a bond is a loan
exercises.explain: Stock means you own part of a company and share in profits. A bond means you lent money and receive fixed interest payments.
choices: A stock is ownership; a bond is a loan
A bond is ownership; a stock is a loan

exercises.question: Generally, which is riskier: stocks or bonds?
exercises.answer: Stocks are riskier; bonds are more stable
exercises.explain: Bond payments are set in advance, and if the borrower stays sound you get your principal back. Stock prices have no such promise, so they tend to be less stable.
choices: Stocks are riskier; bonds are more stable
Risk depends only on the price

exercises.question: What does it mean if a bond issuer has 'poor credit'?
exercises.answer: They might not pay the interest or return your principal
exercises.explain: Poor credit means a history of failing to pay debts on time. Investors worry the borrower might default on the bond.
choices: They might not pay the interest or return your principal
The bond price will always go up

exercises.question: Why might an investor choose a bond over a stock?
exercises.answer: Bonds offer stable, predictable income with lower risk
exercises.explain: Bonds pay fixed interest and are typically lower risk. Stocks are volatile but offer higher potential returns. Different investors have different needs.
choices: Bonds offer stable, predictable income with lower risk
Bonds are issued only once per year

exercises.question: If a bond issuer goes bankrupt, what happens to your bond?
exercises.answer: You might lose part or all of your investment
exercises.explain: If the borrower cannot pay, you may not receive interest or your principal back. This is why credit quality matters for bonds.
choices: You might lose part or all of your investment
You become the owner of the company

units.title: Risk and Return
units.tip: Risk is the chance you lose money. Higher potential returns usually come with higher risk. Risk comes in many forms: market volatility, company failure, inflation. Risk tolerance and time horizon are the two ideas people use to think about how much risk fits a goal.

exercises.question: What is investment risk?
exercises.answer: The chance that your investment loses value or you lose money
exercises.explain: Risk means uncertainty. You might gain or lose. A truly guaranteed return would carry no risk, while a volatile stock carries a lot.
choices: The chance that your investment loses value or you lose money

exercises.question: What is the relationship between risk and potential return?
exercises.answer: Higher risk investments offer higher potential returns
exercises.explain: To attract investors to risky investments, they must offer the possibility of bigger gains. Safe investments offer smaller returns.
choices: Higher risk investments offer higher potential returns
Risk and return are the same thing

exercises.question: You invest 1,000 dollars. The investment returns 10% in year one. How much do you have?
exercises.answer: 1,100 dollars
exercises.explain: 1,000 times 1.10 (meaning 110%) equals 1,100. A 10% return adds 100 dollars to your original 1,000.

exercises.question: What is volatility?
exercises.answer: How much an investment's price swings up and down
exercises.explain: Volatile investments jump around in value. Stable investments move less. High volatility means high uncertainty and high risk.
choices: How much an investment's price swings up and down

exercises.question: Why do investors demand higher returns for riskier investments?
exercises.answer: To compensate for the higher chance of loss
exercises.explain: If an investment has a 50% chance of losing money, investors need the possibility of large gains to justify taking that risk.
choices: To compensate for the higher chance of loss

exercises.question: What is 'risk tolerance'?
exercises.answer: How much investment volatility you can handle emotionally and financially
exercises.explain: Risk tolerance is personal. Some people sleep fine while stocks drop 50%; others panic. Your tolerance shapes your investment choices.
choices: The maximum loss a company can have
How much investment volatility you can handle emotionally and financially

exercises.question: How does time horizon affect investment risk?
exercises.answer: A longer horizon gives more time to ride out downturns
exercises.explain: If money is needed in 2 years, a drop can hurt. With 30 years there is more time for prices to recover from downturns, though recovery is never guaranteed.
choices: Shorter time horizons make risk matter less
A longer horizon gives more time to ride out downturns
Time horizon has no effect on risk

exercises.question: An investor will need a sum of money in 1 year. Which concern matters most for that sum?
exercises.answer: Avoiding large losses, since there is little time to recover
exercises.explain: With a 1-year deadline, a large loss may not have time to recover, so stability matters more than chasing high returns.
choices: Avoiding large losses, since there is little time to recover
Owning as many stocks as possible

exercises.question: A sum is held for 40 years before it is needed. What does the long horizon change?
exercises.answer: There is more time to ride out downturns
exercises.explain: Over 40 years, short-term drops have more time to recover, so they matter less to the end result. Risk does not disappear and recovery is not guaranteed.
choices: There is more time to ride out downturns
It makes the investment stop fluctuating

exercises.question: Which idea is central to thinking about risk?
exercises.answer: Match your investments to your time horizon and risk tolerance
exercises.explain: Risk is judged against two personal factors: when the money is needed and how much volatility the holder can bear.
choices: Match your investments to your time horizon and risk tolerance

units.title: Diversification
units.tip: Diversification means spreading your money across different types of investments so that one bad investment does not ruin your whole portfolio. A diverse portfolio reduces overall risk without giving up as much potential return.

exercises.question: What is diversification?
exercises.answer: Spreading investments across different types of assets to reduce risk
exercises.explain: Instead of putting all your money in one stock, you own multiple stocks, bonds, and other assets. If one fails, others might succeed.
choices: Buying as much as possible of one stock
Spreading investments across different types of assets to reduce risk

exercises.question: You invest 10,000 dollars entirely in one company stock. The company fails. What happens?
exercises.answer: You lose most or all of your 10,000 dollars
exercises.explain: With no diversification, one failure means total loss. This is why 'do not put all eggs in one basket' is investing wisdom.
choices: Your loss is limited to 1,000 dollars
You lose most or all of your 10,000 dollars
You still earn profit because others own the stock

exercises.question: A portfolio of 10,000 dollars is split equally among 10 stocks. One stock fails completely. What is the likely outcome?
exercises.answer: You lose roughly 1,000 dollars, but keep the other 9,000 dollars
exercises.explain: Each stock is 10% of your portfolio. One failure costs you about 10%, not 100%. Diversification limits damage.
choices: You lose roughly 1,000 dollars, but keep the other 9,000 dollars
You gain money from the failure

exercises.question: What asset classes can you diversify across?
exercises.answer: Stocks, bonds, real estate, and cash are all different classes
exercises.explain: Asset classes are different types of investments. Holding multiple classes means your money is not all affected the same way by market changes.
choices: Stocks, bonds, real estate, and cash are all different classes

exercises.question: Does diversification guarantee you will not lose money?
exercises.answer: No, but it reduces the damage from any single investment failure
exercises.explain: Diversification does not prevent all losses, but it prevents one bad investment from destroying your entire portfolio.
choices: No, but it reduces the damage from any single investment failure

exercises.question: What does it mean if two investments are 'positively correlated'?
exercises.answer: They tend to move in the same direction
exercises.explain: If stocks A and B are positively correlated, when one goes up, the other usually goes up too. Poor diversification if both are positively correlated.
choices: One is a stock and one is a bond
They are from the same company
They tend to move in the same direction

exercises.question: Which makes for better diversification?
exercises.answer: Owning investments that do not all move together
exercises.explain: If you own assets that are not perfectly correlated, some will gain when others lose, smoothing out your overall results.
choices: Owning investments that do not all move together
Owning only one type of stock

exercises.question: If you own mostly tech stocks and the tech sector crashes, what happens?
exercises.answer: Most of your portfolio loses value because it is concentrated in one sector
exercises.explain: Holding mostly one sector means one bad sector affects most of your money. Diversification spreads across sectors.
choices: Most of your portfolio loses value because it is concentrated in one sector

exercises.question: Why do some investors limit how much goes into any single holding?
exercises.answer: So one failure cannot do outsized damage to the whole portfolio
exercises.explain: If one position is very large, its failure can wreck the whole portfolio. Capping position size spreads that risk.
choices: So one failure cannot do outsized damage to the whole portfolio
Because large holdings cannot be sold
Because rules require equal amounts in every holding

exercises.question: What is 'rebalancing'?
exercises.answer: Adjusting your portfolio back to your target allocation when prices shift
exercises.explain: If one holding rises from 10% to 15% of a portfolio, rebalancing moves it back toward the target, which keeps the intended level of risk.
choices: Adjusting your portfolio back to your target allocation when prices shift

units.title: Index Funds and Stock Picking
units.tip: An index fund owns shares in many companies, tracking a market index. Picking individual stocks means choosing specific companies. Studies often find that many active stock pickers fail to beat a matching index fund over long periods, mostly because of fees and costs.

exercises.question: What is an index fund?
exercises.answer: A fund that owns shares in many companies, tracking a market index
exercises.explain: An index fund holds stock in the many companies of a market index. It automatically gives broad diversification.
choices: A fund that owns shares in many companies, tracking a market index
A fund managed by a single person picking stocks

exercises.question: What does it mean for a fund to 'track an index'?
exercises.answer: Own the same stocks in the same proportions as the index
exercises.explain: An index fund holds the same stocks in about the same proportions as the index, so its results closely follow the index.
choices: Avoid the stocks in the index
Beat the index by picking better stocks
Own the same stocks in the same proportions as the index

exercises.question: What is a market index?
exercises.answer: A measured basket of stocks used to represent a market
exercises.explain: An index measures how a chosen group of stocks performs as a whole, which is why index funds can be built to follow one.
choices: A measured basket of stocks used to represent a market

exercises.question: What are the advantages of index funds?
exercises.answer: Low fees, broad diversification, and you do not need to pick stocks
exercises.explain: Index funds are cheap to run, automatically diversified across many companies, and take the guesswork out of investing.
choices: Low fees, broad diversification, and you do not need to pick stocks

exercises.question: If a market index rises 8% in a year and you own a fund that tracks it, what do you earn?
exercises.answer: Approximately 8% minus fund fees
exercises.explain: A tracking fund earns roughly the index return. Fees are typically low for index funds, so the result is slightly under 8%.
choices: Depends on what the manager chooses

exercises.question: What does it mean to 'pick stocks'?
exercises.answer: Choose specific company stocks yourself rather than own an index fund
exercises.explain: Stock picking means researching companies and deciding which ones to buy. You hope your picks outperform the overall market.
choices: Choose specific company stocks yourself rather than own an index fund

exercises.question: Over long periods, what do studies commonly find about active managers versus a matching index fund?
exercises.answer: Most active managers fail to beat the index after fees
exercises.explain: A common finding is that most active managers trail a comparable index fund over long periods once fees are counted. Few beat it consistently.
choices: Most active managers fail to beat the index after fees
Nearly all of them beat it

exercises.question: Why do many stock pickers fail to beat index funds?
exercises.answer: High fees, trading costs, and difficulty timing the market correctly
exercises.explain: Professional managers charge fees that eat into returns. Trading frequently costs money. And predicting which stocks will win is hard.
choices: High fees, trading costs, and difficulty timing the market correctly

exercises.question: Is stock picking impossible to do successfully?
exercises.answer: Some people pick winning stocks, but results vary and luck plays a role
exercises.explain: A few stock pickers do outperform the market, but luck plays a large role, and it is hard to know ahead of time who will win.
choices: Yes, no one can ever pick winners
Index funds always outperform all stocks
Some people pick winning stocks, but results vary and luck plays a role

exercises.question: What is the 'core and satellite' approach?
exercises.answer: Holding broad index funds as the core, with a small portion for individual picks
exercises.explain: Core and satellite splits a portfolio into a broad, diversified core and a smaller part used for individual picks.
choices: Picking stocks exclusively and never holding index funds
Holding broad index funds as the core, with a small portion for individual picks

units.title: Time and Compounding
units.tip: Compounding means your returns earn returns. Money grows exponentially over decades, not linearly. Time and staying invested are what give compounding its power.

exercises.question: What is compound interest?
exercises.answer: Earning interest on your interest, creating exponential growth
exercises.explain: Year 1: you earn interest on your principal. Year 2: you earn interest on principal plus year 1's interest. The growth accelerates.
choices: Earning interest on your interest, creating exponential growth

exercises.question: You invest 1,000 dollars at 10% annual return. After 1 year, how much do you have?
exercises.answer: 1,100 dollars
exercises.explain: 1,000 plus 10% of 1,000 equals 1,000 plus 100 equals 1,100 dollars.

exercises.question: After year 1 at 10% you have 1,100 dollars. After year 2 at 10%, how much do you have?
exercises.answer: 1,210 dollars
exercises.explain: 1,100 plus 10% of 1,100 equals 1,100 plus 110 equals 1,210. Your interest earned interest.

exercises.question: You start with 5,000 dollars earning 7% per year. Which timeline shows the biggest growth?
exercises.answer: 30 years
exercises.explain: Compound growth accelerates. At 7% a year, 5,000 dollars becomes about 9,800 after 10 years and about 38,000 after 30 years.

exercises.question: What is the 'Rule of 72'?
exercises.answer: Divide 72 by your annual return percentage to estimate how long to double your money
exercises.explain: At 8% annual return, 72/8 equals 9 years to double. At 6%, 72/6 equals 12 years. It is a quick way to think about compounding.
choices: Your money doubles in exactly 72 years
Divide 72 by your annual return percentage to estimate how long to double your money
Divide 100 by your return to find total profit

exercises.question: Why does starting to invest early matter so much?
exercises.answer: You give compound interest decades to work, multiplying your money many times
exercises.explain: At a steady 8% a year, an extra decade of compounding multiplies the final amount by about 2.2 (1.08 to the 10th power). Earlier money has longer to earn returns on returns.
choices: Age has no effect on returns
You give compound interest decades to work, multiplying your money many times

exercises.question: You invest 100 dollars at age 25, earning 8% per year until age 65. Approximately how much do you have?
exercises.answer: About 2,200 dollars
exercises.explain: 100 times 1.08 to the 40th power is about 2,172. As a check, 72/8 = 9 years per doubling, so 40 years is a bit over 4 doublings, about 21 times the start.

exercises.question: Which statement about long-term investing is most accurate?
exercises.answer: Short-term volatility matters less when you have decades to recover
exercises.explain: A crash early in a 40-year span has many years to recover or be offset. It is a setback, not necessarily the end result.
choices: Time does not affect investment returns
Volatility matters the same regardless of time horizon
Short-term volatility matters less when you have decades to recover

exercises.question: What is dollar-cost averaging?
exercises.answer: Investing the same amount regularly regardless of the stock price
exercises.explain: Instead of trying to time the market, you invest a fixed amount every month. You buy more shares when prices are low, fewer when high.
choices: Investing only when you think the price is lowest
Investing the same amount regularly regardless of the stock price

exercises.question: Which factors make compounding work harder?
exercises.answer: More time and returns left invested
exercises.explain: Compounding grows with time and with returns staying invested to earn further returns. Withdrawals interrupt it and timing is not required.
choices: More time and returns left invested
